title: ``Noisier'’ Noise Contrastive Estimation is (Almost) Maximum Likelihood
claim: The objective landscape is multimodal, with several separated maxima, so local search or estimation can get trapped.
layout: 1 panel, contour map with colorbar at right, green maxima markers
description: A single 2-D contour plot of a multimodal function over axes X1 (about -5 to 10) and X2 (0 to 15). Dense contour lines use a rainbow colormap. Red lines near the top of the scale surround local optima. Blue and purple lines mark very low values at the lower-left and top-center. A vertical colorbar on the right runs from -5 to about -275. Three green dots mark the maxima: top-left, bottom-center and bottom-right. A small legend labelled 'Maxima' sits in the lower right. The eye goes first to the red closed contours around the green dots, then to the steep color gradient. The plot has no arrows, panels or method boxes. It looks like a generic test-function landscape, not the Gaussian gradient-convergence figure the caption describes.
caption: \textbf{"Noisier" \acs{nce} gradients approach the \acs{mle} gradients.} As a sanity check, we simulate the results using 2d Gaussian distributions; true \acs{mle} gradients can be analytically computed. In [ref], we can see that $M \to \infty$ leads to a trajectory-wise convergence from \ac{nce} to \acs{mle}. In [ref], as the noise magnitude $M$ increases, "noisier" \acs{nce} gradients $\nabla_{\bA}\LL_{M}^{{{\rm NCE}}}$ approach \acs{mle} gradients $\nabla_{\bA} \cJ^{\rm MLE}$; bias decaying in the order of $O(\tfrac{1}{M^2})$, which is consistent with [ref]. Further details can be found in [ref].
abstract: Noise Contrastive Estimation (NCE) has fueled major breakthroughs in representation learning and generative modeling. Yet a long-standing challenge remains: accurately estimating ratios between distributions that differ substantially, which significantly limits the applicability of NCE on modern high-dimensional and multimodal datasets. We revisit this problem from a less explored perspective: the magnitude of the noise distribution. Specifically, we show that with a virtually scaled (\ie, artificially increased) noise magnitude, the gradient of the NCE objective can closely align with that of Maximum Likelihood, enabling a trajectory-wise approximation from NCE to MLE, and faster convergence both theoretically and empirically. Building on this insight, we introduce ``Noisier'' NCE, a simple drop-in modification to vanilla NCE that incurs little to no extra computational cost, while effectively handling density-ratio estimation in challenging regimes where traditional MLE and NCE struggle. Beyond improving classical density-ratio learning, ``Noisier'' NCE proves broadly applicable: it achieves strong results across image modeling, anomaly detection, and offline black-box optimization. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet64x64 datasets, it yields 10-step and even 1-step samplers that match or surpass state-of-the-art methods, while cutting training iterations by up to half.
